evidence: Ov. M. 15.416–417: sīc et cūralium quō prīmum contigit aurās tempore, dūrēscit
terms.comment: Pliny’s and Ovid’s word, from the Greek κουράλιον. Pliny knows the red coral of the Mediterranean, that it grows like a shrub and hardens in the air, and that the Indians prize it as Romans prize pearls. Lewis & Short heads it in the other spelling: see the next term.

phrases.latin: sīc et cūralium quō prīmum contigit aurās tempore, dūrēscit: mollis fuit herba sub undīs.
phrases.english: so coral too hardens the moment it touches the air: under the water it was a soft plant.

phrases.latin: ajunt tāctū prōtinus lapidēscere, sī vīvat
phrases.english: they say that, if it is alive, it turns to stone at once when touched
Don’t touch the coral: it’s alive.

long-u.against: Lewis & Short cū^rā^lium, with both vowels common
long-u.html: Ovid scans the word in Met. 15.416: sīc et | cūrali|um quō | prīmum | contigit | aurās, where the second foot is a dactyl cū-ra-li (the et before it is long by position). The long ū answers the Ionic Greek κουράλιον; the a is left unmarked.

sources: Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. coral.
